title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF
subtitle: The little notation that Internet specifications use to say exactly what is allowed.
summary: ABNF (Augmented Backus-Naur Form) is a compact notation for writing down the exact syntax of a protocol message or text format. Rules are built from names, quoted strings, numeric character values, alternatives, repetition and groups. RFC 5234 defines the notation, gives a core set of reusable rules such as ALPHA, DIGIT and CRLF, and even describes ABNF in ABNF. It is the standard way later RFCs, including those for email, URIs and HTTP, specify their grammars.

eli5.summary: It is a set of recipe-card rules for spelling out exactly which words and letters are allowed, so that everyone building a program reads the same message the same way.

tldr.problem: Every protocol specification needs a precise way to say which text is valid, and each one used to re-describe its own notation.
tldr.mechanism: ABNF defines rules of the form name = elements, built with concatenation, / alternatives, =/ incremental alternatives, %x value ranges, repetition prefixes, ( ) groups, [ ] options and ; comments, plus a core rule set in Appendix B.
tldr.outcome: One shared, citable notation lets specification writers and parser authors read and write grammars the same way, and it is used throughout modern Internet standards.

today: ABNF is everywhere in the RFC series. The grammars for internet message headers (RFC 5322), URIs (RFC 3986) and HTTP (RFC 9110) are all written in it, and tools exist that turn ABNF into parsers or check that a grammar is well formed. RFC 7405 later added a way to mark a quoted string as case sensitive, which RFC 5234 itself does not offer.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Internet specifications often need to define a formal syntax, and they are free to use whatever notation their authors like. Over the years a modified Backus-Naur Form, called Augmented BNF or ABNF, became popular. In the early days of the Arpanet each specification carried its own definition of ABNF, notably the email specifications RFC 733 and then RFC 822, which became the usual things to cite.

RFC 5234 pulls that definition out into a document of its own so that any specification can reference it selectively. It also makes some modifications and enhancements. The RFC lists the differences from standard BNF as involving naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence and value ranges.

Appendix B supplies core rule definitions and an encoding for a lexical analyzer of the kind common to several Internet specifications. The RFC says it is a convenience, separate from the ABNF meta-language and from its formal status.
sections.eli5: Long ago, every rulebook explained how to read rules in its own way. This document writes the how-to-read-the-rules page once, so every rulebook can just point to it.

sections.title: Rule Definition
sections.content:
A rule is written as name = elements followed by an end-of-line (a carriage return and line feed). The name is a sequence of characters that starts with a letter and continues with letters, digits and hyphens. Names are case insensitive, so rulename, Rulename, RULENAME and rUlENamE all mean the same rule.

Unlike original BNF, angle brackets around names are not required, though they may be used where they help, typically in running prose or to show partial rules that combine into a string with no white space between them. Rule definitions are left aligned, and a rule that needs several lines continues on indented lines.

The equals sign separates the name from the definition. The elements on the right are one or more rule names or terminal specifications, combined with the operators described in section 3.

Rule names are case insensitive, but that is a separate matter from quoted strings, which have their own case rule covered next.
sections.eli5: Each rule is a name tag, an equals sign, and a description of what the name means. You can write the name in big or small letters and it is still the same name.

sections.title: Terminal Values and External Encodings
sections.content:
Rules eventually resolve into a string of terminal values, often called characters. In ABNF a character is just a non-negative integer. Terminals are written as numbers with an explicit base letter after a percent sign: b for binary, d for decimal and x for hexadecimal. So CR = %d13 and CR = %x0D both name carriage return in US-ASCII.

A period joins values into a concatenated string, so CRLF = %d13.10. Literal text can also be quoted, as in command = "command string", and such strings are interpreted as printable US-ASCII characters.

Quoted strings are case insensitive. rulename = "abc" and rulename = "aBc" both match abc, Abc, ABC and every other mixture. To demand an exact case, spell the characters out as numbers, such as %d97.98.99, which matches only lowercase abc.

How those integers are written on the wire is a separate question. The same grammar may have several external encodings, such as 7-bit US-ASCII, a binary octet environment, or 16-bit Unicode. Encoding is beyond the scope of ABNF, although Appendix B gives definitions for the 7-bit US-ASCII case common on the Internet.
sections.eli5: A letter can be written down as a number, like a secret code where A is 65. ABNF lets you say either the letter in quotes or its number. Quotes do not care about big or small letters, but numbers do.

sections.title: Operators
sections.content:
The RFC defines the building blocks used on the right of a rule. Concatenation is just listing elements one after another, so mumble = foo bar foo matches aba when foo is %x61 and bar is %x62. A slash separates alternatives. The form =/ adds alternatives to an earlier rule, so a list can be built up in fragments.

A dash gives a range of values, as in DIGIT = %x30-39. A numeric value may use dotted concatenation or one dash range, but not both in the same string. Parentheses group elements into one, square brackets make a sequence optional ([foo bar] is the same as *1(foo bar)), and a semicolon starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.

Repetition is written <a>*<b>element, meaning at least a and at most b occurrences. The defaults are 0 and infinity, so *element allows any number including none, and 1*element requires at least one. A bare number n means exactly n, so 2DIGIT is a two-digit number.

ABNF deliberately provides no implicit linear white space. A grammar that wants white space around delimiters has to say so explicitly.
sections.eli5: There are only a few tools: put things in a row, pick one of several, repeat something some number of times, make something optional, and put things in brackets to treat them as one. With those you can describe almost any pattern.

sections.title: Operator Precedence
sections.content:
When several operators appear in one rule, they bind in a fixed order. The RFC lists them from tightest to loosest: rule name, prose value and terminal value; then comments; then value range; then repetition; then grouping and optional; then concatenation; and finally alternative.

The consequence is that concatenation binds more tightly than alternation. The RFC shows that elem (foo / bar) blat matches either elem foo blat or elem bar blat, while elem foo / bar blat matches either elem foo or bar blat.

Mixing alternatives freely with concatenations can be confusing. The RFC strongly advises using explicit grouping, for example (elem foo) / (bar blat), so that casual readers do not misread the rule.
sections.eli5: If a rule has lots of parts, some parts stick together tighter than others, like how in arithmetic multiplication happens before addition. When in doubt, add brackets so nobody has to guess.

sections.title: ABNF Definition of ABNF
sections.content:
Section 4 defines ABNF using ABNF itself. A rulelist is one or more rules or blank or comment lines. A rule is a rulename, a defined-as (either = or =/), its elements and a newline. An alternation is concatenations separated by /, a concatenation is repetitions separated by white space, and each repetition is an optional repeat prefix followed by an element.

An element is a rule name, a group, an option, a quoted char-val, a numeric num-val or a prose-val. The last is a description in angle brackets, which the RFC says is to be used as a last resort, when a formal rule cannot be written.

The RFC notes that this syntax needs a fairly strict formatting of rules, so a ruleset copied from a specification might need preprocessing before an ABNF parser can read it. It also says the grammar uses the core rules from Appendix B.
sections.eli5: The rulebook for writing rules is itself written using those same rules. It is like a dictionary that has a definition for the word dictionary.

sections.title: Core Rules
sections.content:
Appendix B.1 defines a small set of uppercase rules that many Internet specifications reuse. The RFC points out that they are valid for ABNF encoded in 7-bit ASCII or in a character set that is a superset of it. Examples include ALPHA (%x41-5A / %x61-7A), DIGIT (%x30-39), HEXDIG, SP (%x20), HTAB (%x09), WSP (SP / HTAB), CR (%x0D), LF (%x0A), CRLF (CR LF), DQUOTE (%x22), VCHAR (%x21-7E) and OCTET (%x00-FF).

CHAR is any 7-bit US-ASCII character excluding NUL, and CTL is %x00-1F / %x7F. The rule LWSP permits lines containing only white space, which are no longer legal in mail headers. The RFC says not to use it when defining mail headers and to use it with caution elsewhere.

Appendix B.2 says that externally the data are "network virtual ASCII", meaning 7-bit US-ASCII in an 8-bit field with the high bit zero, in network byte order.
sections.eli5: There is a small box of ready-made pieces, such as "a letter", "a digit" and "a new line". Rule writers grab them from the box instead of building them again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section of RFC 5234 is a single sentence, which says that security is truly believed to be irrelevant to this document. ABNF is a notation for writing specifications, not a protocol that carries data between machines.

That does not mean grammars never matter for security. A grammar that is vague or loosely read can lead different implementations to parse the same input differently, and that is often a source of real problems. A precise, shared notation is one way to reduce that risk, although the RFC makes no such claim itself.
sections.eli5: This is a way of writing instructions, not a thing that sends secrets around, so the authors thought there was nothing to protect here.

data.title: A few rules from the RFC
data.code:
CR          =  %x0D
CRLF        =  CR LF
DIGIT       =  %x30-39
foo         =  %x61           ; a
bar         =  %x62           ; b
mumble      =  foo bar foo    ; matches "aba"
ruleset     =  alt1 / alt2
ruleset     =/ alt3
ruleset     =/ alt4 / alt5    ; same as alt1 / alt2 / alt3 / alt4 / alt5
